news.title: German legend goes all out against Argentina: "It didn’t have much to do with football"
news.lede: The Argentina national team once again found itself at the center of international debate. This time, the criticism came from Germany and had Rudi Völler as its main figure. The historic world champion from Italy 1990 and current sporting director of the German Football Federation (DFB) harshly questioned the style of play of the team managed by Lionel Scaloni. Völler took advantage of his speech at the BDFL International Coaches Congress to launch harsh criticism at the Argentina National Team and its defensive and offensive play shown at the 2026 World Cup: "I said that, as Germany, we need to defend better.

news.title: Tunisia confirm Moine Chaabani as head coach following disastrous World Cup
news.lede: "His contract is for a period of four years," the FTF said in a press release, confirming reports that had been circulating for several days. Chaabani won the African Champions League twice and five Tunisian league titles with Esperance Tunis and has also coached in Egypt and then in Morocco, where he won the league title with RS Berkane. Berkane had already said Chaabani was taking over Tunisia. The 45-year-old Tunisian is his country's fourth coach this year and eighth since January 2024.

news.title: Is the World Cup for sale? Here’s what Fifa’s plans mean and what happens next | Paul MacInnes
news.lede: Gianni Infantino is under fire from Uefa over plans to sell off commercial rights for the tournament but he says they are ‘about the democratisation of football worldwide’. A week after the World Cup finished, Fifa has yet to announce whether Argentina will be punished for the violence seen on the pitch at the end of the final. What it has been able to do, however, is devise an entirely new way of running international football, which – in the words of its president, Gianni Infantino – “is about the democratisation of football worldwide”. It is also an idea to allow private investors take a stake in Fifa’s competitions and potentially make money from the World Cup.

news.title: Uefa leads backlash against Infantino's plan to sell stake in World Cup
news.lede: Uefa led the backlash against Fifa after world football's governing body announced plans to seek private investment in the World Cup. Led by president Gianni Infantino, Fifa wants to create a ⁠new commercial subsidiary valued at $20 billion and is seeking backing from its 211 member associations. The plan proposes the creation of the Fifa Forward Enterprise to consolidate the organisation's commercial and event operations. Fifa said it would retain sole control as well as “exclusive authority” over football governance, competitions, the match calendar and all regulatory and sporting decisions.

news.title: The IFAB acknowledged an error in the use of VAR during Argentina-Switzerland and in Embolo's sending-off
news.lede: The controversy over the sending off of Swiss forward Breel Embolo in the match between Argentina and Switzerland in the quarterfinals of the 2026 World Cup added a new chapter. The International Football Association Board (IFAB), the body responsible for establishing the rules of football, indirectly acknowledged that the VAR protocol was applied incorrectly in that play. The incident occurred in the 72nd minute, when the match was tied 1-1. Embolo and Argentine midfielder Leandro Paredes went to challenge for the ball, but the Swiss player fell pretending to have been hit.

news.title: UEFA issues scathing response to Infantino and FIFA’s reported plan to sell World Cup stakes: ‘None of us a...
news.lede: The global soccer landscape suffered a massive shockwave following reports that FIFA president Gianni Infantino plans to sell commercial stakes in the World Cup to private investors. The proposal drew immediate, fierce backlash from rival governing bodies, with European confederation UEFA issuing a blistering response: “None of us are the owners of football.” According to an initial report by The Times‘ Martyn Ziegler, FIFA plans to sell minority equity stakes tied to World Cup commercial rights to private investors. The deal would center on establishing a new commercial subsidiary responsible for managing business and event operations across top men’s and women’s competitions.
